I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette: Yasin, a 34-year-old publisher of Middle Eastern descent, began his days in a cramped office surrounded by stacks of manuscript proofs and the low hum of the copier. The sudden loss of his wife, who was shot to death while she was on a prayer mat in a downtown mosque, had turned his world into a series of flashbacks that arrived with no warning. He was standing on a busy sidewalk, his hand clasping the arm of a stranger as the gunman opened fire; the sound of the gun was drowned by the roar of the city, but the smell of metal and the sight of his wife's face left an imprint that would haunt him for years. In that instant, his life was reduced to a single, incomprehensible point of pain. In the weeks that followed, Yasin found himself reacting violently to a handful of mundane situations that seemed, at first glance, innocuous. The sensation of being naked in a locker room at a local gym, the cramped aisles of the city bus he rode to work, and the constant feeling of exhaustion that clung to him after a restless night would all suddenly flash him back to the mosque. These triggers made him feel exposed and vulnerable, and the next thing he noticed was the threat in the faces around him-familiar strangers now looked menacing, their eyes narrowed in ways that seemed to anticipate an attack. Because of the trigger of bus rides, Yasin began to study faces to detect any potential threat, and he found himself looking for weapons in every public setting, from the security gates at the publishing house to the handrails on the subway platform. The fear that a stranger might conceal a gun in a briefcase drove him to scan every unattended bag, and he would cross himself each time he saw a suspicious object. The memories of that night returned in fragments: a flicker of the white veil of the mosque, the hiss of the gun, the sound of his wife's last word. The sudden appearance of these memories was often accompanied by an auditory echo of the gunshots in his head, as if the sounds were replaying themselves. When the bus was rattling down the highway, Yasin's mind would cut in and re-play the event as a looping film, each frame replayed in the same sequence until he could no longer distinguish past from present. Because of the triggers he experienced on the bus, the memories began to re-surface, and the memory of the gunshot made him even more alert to potential danger. The memories of the event, in turn, fed back into his sense of threat: each time he recalled the image of the gun, he felt his heart pound, and his body went into a state of hypervigilance. The memory of the mosque's flashing lights made the image of the gun more vivid, causing him to feel as though the threat was right there, looming. The more the memories of the event resurfaced, the more he became afraid of the unknown, and the stronger the threat in his mind became. Because of this heightened threat, Yasin began to avoid unfamiliar places. The office he worked in became a strange landscape, the hallway that once seemed ordinary now felt like a maze of potential danger. He started to miss deadlines, feeling the weight of his publisher role crumble. The avoidance of unfamiliar places, in turn, triggered further memories of the event: the emptiness of the hallway mirrored the emptiness he felt in his own life after the loss of his wife. The fear of walking into a new conference room made him feel as if he were stepping into a potential new tragedy. Each avoidance reinforced his sense that the world was a place of constant danger, and that the threat of a new attack loomed large. Yasin's avoidance had real consequences. He started missing book launches, which strained his relationships with authors and editors alike. He found himself declining invitations to speak at industry events, which in turn made him feel increasingly isolated. He would sit at his desk long after hours, his mind cycling through the same looping film, his body tense as he watched colleagues move past him. The combination of constant threat monitoring and intrusive memories had taken a toll on his sleep, and the feeling of fatigue had become a trigger in itself, creating a vicious cycle that only grew tighter. When Yasin finally decided to seek help, it was after an argument with his wife in which she accused him of neglecting their children because he was too absorbed in work. The confrontation made him feel a wave of guilt that was too heavy to bear. He was afraid that if he did not address the distress that had consumed his life, he would lose his career and his marriage. At the same time, he hoped that therapy might allow him to regain control over his thoughts and free himself from the relentless loop of threat, memory, and trigger that had become his reality. The last thing he wanted was to feel the same terror every time he stepped onto a bus or looked at a stranger's face, and the first thing he hoped for was a chance to live again without the weight of the past.
